  ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC’S AND LCRA TRANSMISSION
      SERVICE CORPORATION’S RESPONSE TO JOHN M. BURROW’S
                   APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 25

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (LCRA TSC) (collectively, the “Applicants”) file this response in opposition to John

M. Burrow’s Appeal of SOAH Order No. 25 (the “Appeal”). SOAH Order No. 25 summarily

denied Mr. Burrow’s Motion for Immediate Remedy and Relief relating to notice of the public

participation meetings. For the reasons set forth below, the Commission should deny the Appeal,

because SOAH Order No. 25 is well reasoned, consistent with the Administrative Law Judges’

(ALJs’) ruling in the companion proceeding in Docket No. 59182, and properly applies the

Commission’s Procedural Rule, 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4).

       Mr. Burrow’s Appeal requests that the Commission overrule SOAH Order No. 25 and grant

him and the aligned landowners a day-for-day extension of over 200 days, compel Applicants to

obtain current county tax rolls and notify additional landowners, and compel the ALJs to grant

relief to any newly identified affected property owners. The relief Mr. Burrow seeks would be
 duplicative of the work already performed by Applicants, is legally unfounded, and would cause

severe prejudice to the parties by disrupting a proceeding with a statutory deadline, in which

hundreds of parties have already expended significant time and resources. The Appeal should be

denied for the reasons set forth below.


                                             I.    ARGUMENT

A.      SOAH Order No. 25 is well reasoned and consistent with the ruling in Docket No.
        59182.

        SOAH Order No. 25 correctly denied Mr. Burrow’s motion on two independent grounds.

First, the ALJs found that this matter is subject to the 180-day deadline of the Public Utility

Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.057, and therefore “extension of the procedural schedule is not

feasible.” Second, the ALJs found that Mr. Burrow “did not identify any statute or rule regarding

notice that Applicants failed to comply with.” Moreover, the ALJs’ findings are consistent with

and a prior ruling in the companion proceeding, Docket No. 59182, where Texas Scottish Rite

Hospital (TSRH) raised virtually identical arguments—alleging deficiencies in public

participation meeting notice and seeking a continuance until November 2026. The ALJs rejected

that motion in Docket No. 59182, SOAH Order No. 19, 1 confirming that the statutory deadline

under PURA § 37.057 cannot be circumvented by notice-based delay tactics. Mr. Burrow’s

Appeal presents no materially different legal theory or factual basis that would warrant a different

outcome.




        1
          Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation
to Amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch 765-kV
Transmission Line Project in Crane, Crockett, Irion, Pecos, Reagan, Reeves, Schleicher, Tom Green, Upton, and
Ward Counties, Docket No. 59182, SOAH Order No. 19 (Mar. 26, 2026).



APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO JOHN M. BURROW’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 25
 B.      The statutory deadline under PURA § 37.057 precludes the relief Mr. Burrow seeks.

        The relief Mr. Burrow requests directly conflicts with the statutory deadline governing this

proceeding and therefore cannot be granted. PURA § 37.057 requires the Commission to render

a decision on an application for a new transmission facility within 180 days of filing. This deadline

is mandatory, not discretionary. The Application was filed on March 26, 2026, making the

statutory deadline September 22, 2026. 2 As the ALJs correctly recognized in SOAH Order No.

25, the 180-day deadline renders “extension of the procedural schedule” infeasible. Mr. Burrow’s

request for over 200 additional days would push this proceeding far beyond the statutory deadline.

Mr. Burrow contends that PURA § 37.057 contains a “self-healing remedy” and is in “perfect

harmony” with 16 TAC § 22.52(a). This argument is unpersuasive. The statutory deadline is a

clear legislative directive that the Commission act within 180 days. The fact that PURA § 37.057

permits a party to seek relief in Travis County district court if the Commission fails to act within

180 days does not authorize the Commission or the ALJs to voluntarily extend the proceeding

beyond the statutory deadline. To the contrary, Mr. Howton’s motion must be denied, as it

underscores the legislature’s expectation of timely resolution.

C.      Disrupting the procedural schedule would prejudice all of the parties.

        The procedural schedule adopted in SOAH Order No. 6 on April 20, 2026, was agreed to

by the parties following a prehearing conference on April 14, 2026, and was structured to ensure

compliance with the September 22, 2026 statutory deadline. 3 The hearing on the merits began on

Monday, June 8, 2026 and will continue through Friday, June 12, 2026. The parties have already



         2
           SOAH Order No. 6 Memorializing Prehearing Conference; Granting Request for Good-Cause Exception to
Filing Requirements; Extending Deadline for Comments on Sufficiency of Application and Notice; Adopting
Procedural Schedule; Setting Route Adequacy Hearing, Prehearing Conference, Procedures; and Providing Advisory
to Intervenors Regarding Potential Dismissal at 1–2 (April 20, 2026) (Item No. 788).
        3
            SOAH Order No. 6 at 1–2 (April 20, 2026) (Item No. 788).



APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO JOHN M. BURROW’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 25
 expended significant time and resources preparing for and participating in the hearing on the

merits. More importantly, extending this proceeding and delaying approval of this 765-kV

transmission line would seriously impair the Applicants’ ability to meet the required project in-

service date and cause Applicants to incur additional costs due to these delays. Granting a 200-

day extension at this juncture would impost substantial costs and burdens on all parties.

D.      Applicants met all notice requirements for public meetings.

        16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) requires that “at least one public meeting” be held. 4 Applicants

exceeded this requirement by conducting three meetings in three different counties in June 2025.

In addition to holding multiple public meetings, Applicants published notice of the public

participation meetings in eleven newspapers of general circulation throughout the project study

area on or about June 10–12, 2025. While 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) does not require newspaper

publication of public meeting notices, this additional step further demonstrates that Applicants

went beyond their regulatory obligations to ensure broad notification of the June 2025 public

participation meetings. Further, Applicants mailed notice of the public meeting to landowners

within 520 feet of the centerline of the preliminary alternative route links as stated on the county

tax rolls, exceeding the requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4).

        Mr. Burrow’s request for a day-for-day extension because Applicants did not provide

notice of the public meeting to the landowners affected by Links F04 and F20 misreads the rule.

16 TAC § 22.52(a)(5) states that “[f]ailure to provide notice in accordance with this section will

be cause for day-for-day extension of deadlines for intervention and for commission action on the

application.” 5     This remedy is inapplicable here for two independent reasons.           First, as



        4
            16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4).
        5
            16 TAC § 22.52(a)(5).



APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO JOHN M. BURROW’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 25
 demonstrated above, Applicants fully complied with the notice requirements of 16 TAC

§ 22.52(a)(4). Second, the day-for-day extension provision does not apply to public meeting

notice.

          The day-for-day extension remedy in § 22.52(a)(5) applies to failures to comply with the

notice requirements for filing an application as set forth in 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(1)-(3), specifically,

the requirements to publish notice in newspapers, mail notice to municipalities and directly

affected landowners, and provide proof of notice upon filing. 6 The public participation meeting

requirement of § 22.52(a)(4), by contrast, is a separate, pre-application obligation that is not always

required. The rule mandates a public meeting only if 25 or more persons would be entitled to

receive direct mail notice. Nothing in the text of the rule extends the day-for-day extension remedy

to the public meeting context, and Mr. Burrow has cited no authority to the contrary.

E.        Applicants met all notice requirements for their Application.

          Mr. Burrow’s assertion that newly affected landowners were denied their “right and duty

to be a knowledgeable, prepared, and effective party” is unfounded. There is no requirement that

landowners get advanced notice of an Application prior to the date it is filed. Applicants mailed

notice of the CCN application to landowners within 520 feet of the centerline of the alternative

routes as stated on the county tax rolls, as required by 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3). The ALJs found the

Applicants’ notice sufficient in SOAH Order No. 7. 7

          Mr. Burrow’s interpretation of notice has no foundation in Texas case law. For example,

in McMaster v. Public Utility Commission of Texas, the landowner did not receive a mailed notice

of a CCN application from the applicant and did not request to intervene in the proceeding until



          6
              Id.
          7
              SOAH Order No. 7 Finding Notice and Application Sufficient at 2 (Apr. 21, 2026) (Item No. 1006).



APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO JOHN M. BURROW’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 25
 long after he received actual notice, when the Commission had already issued a final order. 8 The

Commission denied his request to intervene, and the landowner appealed, claiming his due process

rights had been violated because he was entitled to receive a mailed notice from the applicant,

which he never had. 9

        The Court of Appeals of Texas, Austin Division, recognized in that case that, “[a]t a

minimum, due process requires notice and an opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in

a meaningful manner.” 10 The court further confirmed that publication in newspapers and direct

mailing to identified landowners “generally satisfy constitutional requirements” for notice, and

that actual receipt of a mailed notice is not the applicable standard, 11 noting that the Commission’s

own rules make clear that “[t]he lack of actual notice to any individual landowner will not in and

of itself support a finding that the requirements of [the notice provision] have not been satisfied.” 12

The court went on to explain why the landowner’s interpretation of the Commission’s notice

requirements was “absurd”:

                    It would allow a person who had actual knowledge of the CCN
                    proceeding to wait until after resolution of the matter—i.e., after all
                    the other parties expended considerable time and money on the
                    issue—to step forward with a complaint. It would also, in some
                    cases like this one, thwart the statutory directive that the
                    Commission issue an order on the CCN application by the 181st
                    day after the CCN application was filed. Likewise, it would thwart
                    the stated purposes of the Commission’s rules that these
                    proceedings be just and efficient. 13

          Mr. Burrow’s interpretation of the notice rule leads to an equally absurd result. It would

allow a party, such as Mr. Burrow, with actual knowledge of this matter—indeed, one who has

actively participated in it—to disrupt the proceeding after the parties had expended considerable

time and money. It would also thwart the statutory directive that the Commission render a decision

within 180 days after the CCN application was filed and the purpose of the Commission’s rules

that proceedings be just and efficient—all based on notice that was already found sufficient. 14

         Mr. Burrow has had a full and meaningful opportunity to participate in this proceeding.

He intervened as a party, propounded discovery on Applicants, and filed testimony. Similarly,

Mr. David Hillock, who is also identified in Mr. Burrow’s motion, timely intervened and has

participated in this proceeding. 15

F.       Mr. Burrow’s Addendum to his Appeal is improper because it raises new arguments
         not included in his motion below and substantively lacks merit.

         Mr. Burrow’s Addendum 16 raises new arguments that were not properly before the ALJs

with his motion. Specifically, he claims that “[n]ew information has come to light” that Applicants

failed to notice other landowners. 17 Contrary to Mr. Burrow’s allegations, as explained above,

Applicants appropriately noticed directly affected landowners listed on county tax rolls. This

notice was found sufficient in SOAH Order No. 7. 18 As a result of intervenor testimony or

discovery in this proceeding, Applicants became aware of additional landowners who recently

purchased property within 500 feet of the centerline of an alternative route link that were not

3194).

           John M. Burrow’s Addendum to Appeal of SOAH Order No. 25 to the Honorable Public Utility

         17

         18

APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO JOHN M. BURROW’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 25
 identified on the county tax rolls at the time the Application was filed. Applicants have sent

supplemental direct mail notice to these landowners, even if they received actual notice of the

Application and have timely intervened. These supplemental notices are detailed in Applicants’

Affidavit Attesting to the Provisoin of Notice to Municipalities, Utilities, Counties, the Department

of Defense Siting Clearinghouse, OPUC, TPWD, and Landowners and Newspaper Notice 19 as

well as the Supplemental Affidavit Attesting to the Provision of Notice, 20 consistent with the

requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52(F).


                                            II.    CONCLUSION

        For the foregoing reasons, Applicants respectfully request that the Commission deny Mr.

Burrow’s Appeal and uphold SOAH Order No. 25.
